clue.text: Showing the white feather, unlike Richard

explanation.surface: Someone shows cowardice, quite unlike a famously brave king.
explanation.walkthrough: Showing the white feather is an old British idiom for cowardice. King Richard I was called the Lionheart, so a timid heart is the opposite of his.
explanation.definitionFit: A white feather was the old emblem of cowardice, and a timid person is the opposite of Richard the Lionheart.

clue.text: " But me no buts "-a sound if unavailing protest by the duke?

definitions.text: " But me no buts "-a sound if unavailing protest by the duke?

parts.words: " But me no buts "-a sound if unavailing protest by the duke?
parts.note: the duke in Shakespeare's Richard III was drowned in a butt (cask) of malmsey wine, so his plea not to be put in butts sounds like 'but me no buts'

explanation.surface: A stubborn objector cuts off all argument with a stock phrase, in vain.
explanation.walkthrough: Legend says George, Duke of Clarence, brother of Edward IV, was drowned in a butt of malmsey; 'buts' and 'butts' sound the same, so his protest fits the stock phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The royal dukedom borne by George, the brother of Edward IV, who was drowned in a cask of malmsey in the Tower.

clue.text: Exam prospect offered to the job-hunter

parts.note: the Inter, short for intermediate, was a university examination taken between matriculation and finals
a prospect is a view, the scene spread out before you

explanation.surface: A candidate who has passed an exam gets the prospect of a job.
explanation.walkthrough: INTER was the old British intermediate examination, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: An employer grants a meeting with questions to a person seeking work, the usual step before hiring.

clue.text: Steamer captain?

explanation.surface: Who commands the steamship?
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Kettle was the hero of C. J. Cutcliffe Hyne's popular adventure stories, a fiery little steamer skipper.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot that boils water gives off steam, and Captain Kettle was a famous fictional sea skipper.

clue.text: She's barely recognizable

parts.note: barely is read as 'in a bare state': a woman with no clothes on

explanation.surface: Someone is so changed she can hardly be recognised.
explanation.definitionFit: An unclothed figure, as in a painting, is one seen bare.

clue.text: See 1
Farmer has to economize on the island'

parts.note: to husband resources is to use them sparingly
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A farmer must tighten his belt because he lives on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has to' and 'on the' are link words; the Isle of Man is a British island between England and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a tiller of the soil, one who husbands the land.

clue.text: Heavenly bear-keeper

parts.note: a star whose Greek name means guardian of the bear, as it follows the Great Bear across the sky

explanation.surface: A celestial zookeeper looks after a bear.
explanation.walkthrough: The star's name comes from Greek arktos (bear) and ouros (guardian); it sits beside Ursa Major.
explanation.definitionFit: The bright star in Bootes whose Greek name means guardian of the bear.

clue.text: But the Union Jack precedes this union

definitions.text: But the Union Jack precedes this union

parts.words: But the Union Jack precedes this union
parts.note: in the flag's name 'union' comes before 'jack', but in this kind of union the other word comes first: the workers' organisation

explanation.surface: A remark that the national flag should come before an alliance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Union Jack is the British flag. Here the wanted word goes in front of 'union' to name a workers' association.
explanation.definitionFit: Commerce or a craft; its name goes before 'union' to make a labour organisation.

clue.text: Hardy ruler

parts.note: Thomas Hardy wrote the verse drama The ..., about the Napoleonic wars, so a ruler from his title

explanation.surface: A tough, robust monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like an adjective meaning tough; it is the novelist Thomas Hardy, author of The Dynasts.
explanation.definitionFit: A hereditary ruler, as in Thomas Hardy's epic drama The Dynasts.

clue.text: Positions adopted to confound the test audit

indicators.note: to confound is to throw into confusion, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Accountants take up stances to baffle the examination of the books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the' is a link word; the nine letters of TEST AUDIT are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Postures or stances struck by the body, or views held, are positions adopted.

clue.text: A tie-up here with a ball between the wickets

definitions.text: A tie-up here with a ball between the wickets

parts.words: A tie-up here with a ball between the wickets
parts.note: a fetter with an iron ball for a prisoner, and the 22-yard length of a cricket pitch between the wickets, an old surveyor's measure

explanation.surface: A cricket match ends in a tie with the ball between the stumps.
explanation.walkthrough: A cricket pitch is 22 yards from wicket to wicket, exactly one surveyor's measure of that name; a ball and fetter tie up a convict.
explanation.definitionFit: Linked metal fetters tie up a prisoner with ball attached, and the old 22-yard measure equals the length of a cricket pitch.

clue.text: Record one way to prepare a sausage?

parts.words: one way to prepare a sausage?
parts.note: read as French-style cookery, a sausage served '...', as one might say en croute

explanation.surface: A cook describes a method for serving a sausage.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb meaning to put on a register splits as EN ROLL, mock-French for a sausage in a roll; this is the American spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: To put a name on a register or list is to record it.

clue.text: Many a Roman dictator takes us on the staff

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword stand-in for many
Il Duce was the title of Mussolini, the dictator ruling from Rome

explanation.surface: A dictator in Rome takes many of us onto his staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' and 'on the' are link words; 'staff' is a rod, not employees.
explanation.definitionFit: Hermes's herald's wand, entwined with two snakes, is a rod carried as a symbol.

clue.text: Like Uriah in the river, it's gone with the wind

indicators.note: one word set within the other, as Uriah is placed in the river

parts.note: the Tweed is a river on the border of England and Scotland
Uriah Heep in David Copperfield calls himself ''umble', dropping the h of humble

explanation.surface: Uriah is swept away down a river, gone with the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep, the fawning clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield, always says he is ''umble'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant that breaks off and rolls across the prairie, blown by the breeze.

clue.text: Translation cracked by Sikes ?

explanation.surface: A burglar breaks into a translation.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Sikes is the burglar in Dickens's Oliver Twist, and a house to burgle was a 'crib' in thieves' slang; 'to crack a crib' was to break in.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolboy's illicit literal version is a pony, and in thieves' cant a house to rob is cracked by a burglar.

clue.text: " Man — The First Stage " by The Sphinx

definitions.text: " Man — The First Stage " by The Sphinx

parts.words: " Man — The First Stage " by The Sphinx
parts.note: the Sphinx's riddle: man goes on four legs in the morning of life, crawling as a baby

explanation.surface: Reads like the title of a book by an author called the Sphinx.
explanation.walkthrough: The riddle of the Sphinx asks what walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon and three in the evening: man, crawling, walking, then with a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-footed animal, which is how a crawling infant goes in the riddle.

clue.text: Accommodation for bar-lifters

parts.note: drinkers at the bar lift their arms at the joint to raise a glass, so they need space for that joint

explanation.surface: Lodgings for weightlifters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar-lifters' suggests weightlifters; they are drinkers, and 'lifting the elbow' is British slang for drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Space to move freely, literally space for the arm's joint.

clue.text: Objet d'art in return for lubricant gun

indicators.note: in return means these two words are read backwards together

parts.note: oil is a lubricant
gat is old American slang for a pistol

explanation.surface: Someone trades an art object for some gun oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns the lubricant and the gun round as one run, not each separately; 'in return' looks like a phrase meaning 'in exchange', but 'in' gives letters and 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A gem or carving with a design cut into its surface, a collectable work of art.

clue.text: Breakdown gang in the lab

parts.note: not a crew clearing up a crash, but scientists who break substances down into their parts

explanation.surface: A recovery crew works in a laboratory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breakdown gang' suggests a railway or roadside recovery crew; the breaking down is chemical analysis.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemists who work out what something is made of break it down.

clue.text: Vessel gives a fair imitation of that daring young man

definitions.text: Vessel gives a fair imitation of that daring young man

parts.words: Vessel gives a fair imitation of that daring young man
parts.note: a boat-shaped fairground ride rocks to and fro like the daring young man on the flying trapeze

explanation.surface: A ship does a decent impression of a reckless youth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fair' looks like 'reasonable'; it is a fairground. 'The daring young man on the flying trapeze' is a music-hall song.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat-shaped seat hung from a frame at a fairground, which rocks to and fro.

clue.text: As dark as Algernon ?

parts.note: the writer Algernon Blackwood's surname is black wood, the dark timber, which also means jet black

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a thing is as gloomy as a man called Algernon.
explanation.walkthrough: Algernon Blackwood was an English writer of ghost stories; his surname, black wood, is the dark timber whose poetic name also means black.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic word for black, and for the black wood of that name.

clue.text: Two-wheeler misses a duck but gets another

indicators.note: the vehicle misses, that is loses, one letter

parts.note: a scooter is a two-wheeled vehicle
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so the letter O

explanation.surface: A motor scooter swerves to avoid one duck but hits another.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck in cricket is a score of zero, hence O. 'another' is the definition: a different duck, a sea bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark sea duck, so another of the birds after the first one in the clue.

clue.text: This style is not coming back

definitions.text: This style is not coming back

parts.words: This style is not coming back
parts.note: leaving in this nation's manner means slipping away without permission or farewell

explanation.surface: A fashion that will never return.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'take French leave' is to leave without saying goodbye or permission.
explanation.definitionFit: The national adjective in the idiom for a departure without leave.

clue.text: Old Kaspar at home

parts.note: in Southey's poem After Blenheim, Old Kaspar sits at his little country house door at evening

explanation.surface: An old man called Kaspar sits at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Southey's poem After Blenheim opens with Old Kaspar sitting 'before his cottage door'.
explanation.definitionFit: One who lives in a small country dwelling, like Southey's Kaspar.

clue.text: Emperor associated with SEATO perhaps?

explanation.surface: An emperor is linked with the Southeast Asian treaty alliance.
explanation.walkthrough: SEATO was the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization; its letters rearranged spell OATES, and Titus Oates invented the Popish Plot of 1678. 'perhaps' warns that the link is through those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman ruler of the first century, and first name of the plotter Oates, whose surname matches SEATO's letters.

clue.text: Little digger lays it on thick

explanation.surface: A small excavator applies something generously.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'lay it on with a trowel' means to flatter heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand tool for scooping soil, and the plasterer's tool of the idiom for heavy flattery.

clue.text: Sapper's female of the species

parts.note: Sapper was the pen name of H. C. McNeile, whose novel The Female of the Species features the villainess Peterson

explanation.surface: An army engineer's wife or mate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sapper' looks like a military engineer; it is the author of the Bulldog Drummond books, whose villainess is Irma Peterson.
explanation.definitionFit: The first name of the villainess in Sapper's Bulldog Drummond stories.

clue.text: "Head to foot Now is he gules " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "Head to foot Now is he gules " (Hamlet)

parts.words: "Head to foot Now is he gules " (Hamlet)
parts.note: the missing word from the player's speech about Pyrrhus, wholly red with blood from head to foot

explanation.surface: A line quoted from Hamlet with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The First Player in Hamlet says of Pyrrhus: 'Head to foot now is he total gules'; gules is red in heraldry.
explanation.definitionFit: Completely, as Pyrrhus is entirely red with blood from head to foot.

clue.text: Certain to back out — or one might be wrong

indicators.note: out says the reversed word stands outside, around the next letters

parts.note: certain means sure

indicators.note: might be suggests these letters could be rearranged

explanation.surface: Being sure, then backing out, means someone might have been mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to back' turns the word for certain round; 'might be' rearranges 'or one' into the old duplicator brand Roneo; 'out' puts the reversed word around it, splitting it after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistaken or incorrect, as a false belief is.

clue.text: Talk back in the Services ?

parts.note: not insolence in the armed forces, but the congregation answering the priest at church services

explanation.surface: Insubordination in the armed forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Services' suggests the army, navy and air force; it means church services, where a congregation answers the priest.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a reply, as a congregation does to the priest in church.

clue.text: Man-mountain takes me in for domestic occasions

indicators.note: takes in signals one word placed within another

parts.note: Mount Athos in Greece is a monastic mountain where only men may go

explanation.surface: A giant of a man takes me in for some family gatherings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man-mountain' suggests a huge man; it is Mount Athos, a holy mountain closed to women.
explanation.definitionFit: Receptions held in one's own house, when a hostess received callers.
